title: How to Tell How Old Your HVAC System Is
h1: How Can I Tell How Old My HVAC System Is?
description: Find the age of your furnace, AC or heat pump using the data plate and serial number, plus what age means for repairs, efficiency and planning a replacement.
quick_answer: Find the data plate on the furnace, air handler or outdoor unit and read the serial number. Most manufacturers code the year and often the week or month of manufacture into it. If you can't decode it, look for a manufacture date on the label, check permits or paperwork, or ask a technician to look during a tune-up.
body:
Where do I find the data plate?

Every furnace, air handler, air conditioner and heat pump has a metal or sticker label called the rating or data plate. It lists the model number, serial number and electrical information.

  • Outdoor AC or heat pump: usually on a side panel, often near the electrical connections
  • Furnace or air handler: inside the front access panel or on the side of the cabinet. In San Diego and Orange County homes, look in the garage, attic or a hall closet.
  • Package units: on the side of the cabinet, often on the roof or beside the house

Before opening a furnace panel, turn off the service switch. Only look, and don't touch any wiring or the gas valve. Take a photo of the plate so you can read it comfortably and share it later.

How do I read the serial number?

Each brand uses its own format, but most hide the build date in the serial number. Common patterns include:

  • Year first. Some brands start with a four-digit code where the first two digits are the year and the next two are the week, such as 1508 for the 8th week of 2015.
  • Week then year. Others put the week first and the year second.
  • Letter codes. Some use letters to stand for the year and month.
  • Printed dates. Many newer labels simply list a manufacture date.

If the format isn't obvious, the manufacturer's customer service line can usually decode it. A technician who works on several brands can often tell you on the spot.

What if I can't find or read the label?

Labels fade, especially on outdoor units in full Southern California sun. Other ways to estimate age:

  • Check home purchase disclosures or inspection reports
  • Look for installation stickers or service tags on the equipment
  • Search your city or county permit records for past HVAC permits
  • Look at the refrigerant listed on the plate. Systems built for R-22 refrigerant are generally older equipment.

How long do HVAC systems usually last?

Lifespan varies with how hard the system works and how well it's maintained. As a general guide:

EquipmentTypical lifespan
Gas furnaceAbout 15 to 20 years
Central air conditionerAbout 12 to 15 years
Heat pumpAbout 10 to 15 years
DuctworkOften 20 years or more, depending on material and condition

Coastal homes see more corrosion on outdoor coils and cabinets from salt air, which can shorten their life. Inland systems often run harder during long, hot summers. In our mild climate, furnaces often outlast the AC.

Should I repair or replace an older system?

There's no single cutoff, but a few questions help. Is the repair a small part or a major component like a compressor or heat exchanger? Has the system needed several repairs in the last couple of years? Are some rooms always uncomfortable, or are bills climbing even with regular maintenance?

If the answers point to an aging system that's getting less reliable, it often makes more sense to put the repair money toward a replacement. A technician can give you an honest look at both options, along with the age of each part of your system.

What does the age of my system tell me?

Age alone doesn't mean you need a new system, but it helps you plan. Things to think about once equipment gets into the later part of its life:

  • Repairs become more frequent, and parts can be harder to find
  • Older systems are much less efficient than current equipment
  • Older ACs that use R-22 refrigerant can be expensive to recharge
  • A worn furnace heat exchanger should be checked regularly for cracks

It also helps to know which parts are oldest. In many homes the outdoor AC was replaced at some point while the original furnace stayed, or the other way around, so one half of the system may be much closer to the end of its life than the other.

Knowing the age lets you budget and choose your timing instead of replacing in an emergency. Our HVAC technicians can check age and condition during a tune-up, and our heating team can inspect an older furnace before the cold nights arrive.
faqs: Does the age of my HVAC system matter when selling a home?
Often, yes. Buyers and inspectors will note the age of the furnace and AC. A newer system can be a selling point, while an older one may come up during negotiations.
Should I replace my HVAC system just because it is old?
Not necessarily. If an older system runs well, is safe and has been maintained, it can keep going. Weigh the age with repair frequency, efficiency and how comfortable the house is.
Do the indoor and outdoor units have the same age?
Not always. One part may have been replaced on its own. Check the data plate on each unit separately, since they're often different ages.
How do I know if my AC uses R-22 refrigerant?
Look at the data plate on the outdoor unit. It lists the refrigerant type. If it says R-22 or HCFC-22, the system is older and refrigerant for it is limited and costly.
